title: Kartarpur corridor, 2019
hookLine: a corridor opens so pilgrims from India can visit Kartarpur, where Nanak farmed

lines: A WHITE GURDWARA, FOUR KILOMETERS AWAY.
cards: For years, at a town called Dera Baba Nanak, right on the Indian side of the border, there was a viewing platform. Pilgrims climbed up, some with binoculars, and looked across the fields.
About four kilometers away, just visible on a clear day, stood a white gurdwara in Pakistan. People bowed to a building they could see but couldn't reach. Some came back year after year.
Some grew old doing it. Then, in November 2019, a road opened.

teach.b: Kartarpur means the Creator's town. Guru Nanak founded it on the bank of the river Ravi after his long journeys, and spent the last years of his life there, about eighteen of them. What did he do there?
He farmed. The Guru who had spent some twenty years on the road, across India and, tradition says, as far as Mecca and Baghdad, came home and worked the fields.
Around him grew the first Sikh community: people who worked honestly, sang together morning and evening, and ate together.
There Guru Nanak passed the light to Guru Angad, and there he died, in 1539. In 1947 the border put Kartarpur on the Pakistani side: close enough to see, too far to touch.
Then, in 2019, the two governments opened a corridor: a road, a bridge and a crossing, so pilgrims from India could walk to the gurdwara without a visa and come back the same day.
It opened on the ninth of November, days before the five hundred fiftieth anniversary of Guru Nanak's birth. People wept at the crossing. Old men who had stood on the platform for decades walked in.
It hasn't been simple. The corridor has closed at times, during the pandemic and in periods of tension between the two countries.
But for Sikhs it answered, in part, the prayer said every day since 1947.

And it closes our long walk through Sikh history: from Banda Singh and the years in the forests, through the Misls and Maharaja Ranjit Singh, annexation and the gurdwara reform, to Partition and a door that opened.

how: Sikh pilgrims from India cross the Kartarpur corridor, when it is open, to visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, where Guru Nanak lived his last years; many Sikhs mark his birth anniversary there.

games.why: a road, a bridge and a crossing opened days before Guru Nanak's 550th birth anniversary, and pilgrims walked in.

practice: If you can, walk, even across the room, to a spot that means something: a window, a photograph, a doorway you love; if you can't move right now, walk there in your mind, step by step.
Notice that you're going toward something, not just away. When you arrive, rest there quietly and let yourself be glad you can reach it.
